source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Context-sensitive Languages (5 hrs)

stem: Compared with a CFG derivation, a CSG derivation of w has length:
options: Bounded — since forms never shrink, at most exponentially many distinct steps up to |w|
explanation: Monotone growth caps derivation search.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Context-sensitive Languages (5 hrs)

topic: Linear bounded automata and equivalence with CSG
stem: The LBA model was introduced by:
options: Myhill (studied further by Landweber and Kuroda)
explanation: Myhill 1960; Kuroda tied NLBAs to CSGs in 1964.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Context-sensitive Languages (5 hrs)

topic: The basic model for Turing machines (TM)
stem: A Turing machine consists of:
options: A finite control, an infinite tape and a read/write head that can move both ways
explanation: The 1936 model — the standard formalization of computation.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: The basic model for Turing machines (TM)
stem: A TM transition δ(q, X) = (p, Y, R) means:
options: Read X in state q, write Y, move right, enter state p
explanation: One step = read/write/move/state-change.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: The basic model for Turing machines (TM)
stem: TMs differ from LBAs and PDAs most fundamentally by having:
explanation: Unlimited storage — the source of full computational power.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: The basic model for Turing machines (TM)
stem: A TM 'configuration' (instantaneous description) records:
options: The state, tape contents and head position
explanation: Everything needed to continue the computation.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Turing recognizable (Recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages and the
stem: A language is DECIDABLE (recursive) when some TM:
options: Accepts it and may loop otherwise
Halts on EVERY input, accepting exactly the members
explanation: Total deciders answer yes/no always.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Turing recognizable (Recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages and the
stem: A language is RECOGNIZABLE (recursively enumerable) when some TM:
options: Accepts exactly its members but may LOOP on non-members
explanation: Semi-decision: yes answers guaranteed, no answers possibly never.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Turing recognizable (Recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages and the
stem: L is decidable if and only if:
options: Both L and its complement are recognizable
explanation: Run both recognizers in parallel — one must halt (Post's theorem).
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Turing recognizable (Recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages and the
stem: The complement of a recognizable but undecidable language is:
explanation: Otherwise both halves recognizable ⇒ decidable — contradiction.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: Multi-tape Turing machines compared with single-tape TMs are:
options: Equal in computing power (with at most polynomial slowdown when simulated)
explanation: Robustness of the model — variants all collapse to the same power.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: A TM with a two-way infinite tape can be simulated by a one-way infinite tape TM by:
options: Folding the tape into two tracks
explanation: Track-pairing — the standard simulation.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Nondeterministic TMs and equivalence with deterministic TMs
stem: Nondeterministic TMs accept:
options: Exactly the same class of languages (with possibly exponential slowdown)
explanation: Breadth-first simulation of the computation tree preserves the language class.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Nondeterministic TMs and equivalence with deterministic TMs
stem: The deterministic simulation of an NTM explores the computation tree:
options: Breadth-first (or iterative deepening) to guarantee finding accepting paths
explanation: DFS could dive into a non-halting branch — BFS is safe.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Unrestricted grammars and equivalence with Turing machines
stem: Unrestricted (Type-0) grammars generate exactly:
options: The recursively enumerable languages — precisely what TMs recognize
explanation: Grammar derivations simulate TM computations and vice versa.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Unrestricted grammars and equivalence with Turing machines
stem: In an unrestricted grammar, the left side of a production may be:
options: Any string containing at least one variable
explanation: Full rewriting freedom — matching TM power.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: An enumerator is a TM that:
options: Prints out strings of a language, possibly with repetitions, on an output tape
explanation: L is RE ⟺ some enumerator lists exactly L (hence 'recursively ENUMERABLE').
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: A language is DECIDABLE iff some enumerator lists it:
explanation: Ordered enumeration lets membership be settled after finitely many outputs.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: The basic model for Turing machines (TM)
stem: The Church-Turing thesis (previewed here) asserts that TMs capture:
options: Everything effectively computable by any mechanical procedure
explanation: A thesis, not a theorem — supported by every proposed model coinciding.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: A queue automaton (FIFO instead of stack) is:
options: Turing-complete — equal in power to TMs
explanation: A queue can simulate a tape — surprising completeness.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Turing recognizable (Recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages and the
stem: Which chain of inclusions is correct?
explanation: Halting-everywhere is stronger than accepting-only; some languages are not even RE.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: The basic model for Turing machines (TM)
stem: True or False: A Turing machine may write on its tape and move its head both left and right.
explanation: True — read/write plus bidirectional movement distinguish it from weaker machines.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Nondeterministic TMs and equivalence with deterministic TMs
stem: True or False: Nondeterminism increases the class of languages Turing machines can recognize.
explanation: False — NTM ≡ DTM in language power (efficiency is the open P vs NP matter).
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Turing recognizable (Recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages and the
stem:
Assertion (A): Running recognizers for L and its complement in parallel decides L.
Reason (R): Every string belongs to exactly one of the two languages, so one machine must halt and accept.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Dovetailing the two semi-deciders yields a total decider — R explains A.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem:
Assertion (A): Adding multiple tapes does not change what is computable.
Reason (R): A single tape can encode k tapes on interleaved tracks with head-position markers.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The classic simulation with quadratic overhead — R explains A.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: Which characterizations of recursively enumerable languages are correct? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: The fourth characterizes DECIDABLE languages — a proper subclass.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: The basic model for Turing machines (TM)
stem: Which components belong to the TM 7-tuple? (Select all that apply.)
options: Tape alphabet Γ containing the blank
explanation: Stacks belong to PDAs; the tape subsumes them.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: The basic model for Turing machines (TM)
stem: The blank symbol of a TM belongs to:
options: The tape alphabet Γ but not Σ
explanation: Blanks pad the tape beyond the input; inputs never contain blanks.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Turing recognizable (Recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages and the
stem: The halting problem language HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w} is:
explanation: Simulate to accept; no decider exists (Turing 1936).
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: A TM with a 'stay' (S) head option in addition to L/R:
options: Is equivalent — S is simulated by R then L
explanation: Another robustness result.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Unrestricted grammars and equivalence with Turing machines
stem: Type-0 languages are also called:
explanation: Generated by unrestricted grammars ≡ accepted by TMs.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: The term 'recursively enumerable' comes from the fact that such languages can be:
explanation: Enumerator characterization gives the class its name.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Nondeterministic TMs and equivalence with deterministic TMs
stem: The computation of an NTM on an input is best pictured as:
options: A tree of configurations branching on nondeterministic choices
explanation: Acceptance = some root-to-accept path exists.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: The basic model for Turing machines (TM)
stem: A TM computing f(n) = n+1 on unary input (n 1s) would typically:
options: Move to the right end of the 1s and append one more 1, then halt
explanation: TMs compute functions as well as accept languages.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Turing recognizable (Recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages and the
stem: Which is DECIDABLE?
explanation: DFA acceptance is decidable by simulation; the TM analogues are not.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: A TM restricted to a tape alphabet of exactly {0, 1, blank}:
options: Retains full power — larger alphabets are encoded in binary blocks
explanation: Alphabet reduction is another equivalence.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Unrestricted grammars and equivalence with Turing machines
stem: Simulating a TM by a grammar encodes:
options: Configurations as sentential forms, with productions mimicking transitions
explanation: Derivation steps = computation steps.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: Dovetailing in enumeration means:
options: Interleaving steps across infinitely many computations so none blocks the rest
Running inputs one by one to completion
explanation: Round-robin simulation — essential when some runs never halt.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: The basic model for Turing machines (TM)
stem: The 'busy beaver' function BB(n) (max steps of halting n-state TMs) is:
options: Uncomputable — it grows faster than every computable function
explanation: Deciding it would solve halting.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Nondeterministic TMs and equivalence with deterministic TMs
stem: P vs NP concerns the cost of removing nondeterminism with respect to:
explanation: Same languages, possibly different polynomial-time status — the million-dollar question.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

topic: Turing recognizable (Recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages and the
stem: Every finite language is:
explanation: Finite lookup decides membership trivially.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: An offline TM (read-only input tape + work tapes) is used mainly to define:
options: Space complexity classes below linear (e.g. LOGSPACE)
explanation: Charging only work-tape space enables sublinear space measures.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Turing Machines (8 hrs)

stem: The Church-Turing thesis asserts that:
options: Every effectively calculable function is computable by a Turing machine
explanation: An identification of intuitive computability with TM computability.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The thesis cannot be PROVEN because:
options: 'Effectively calculable' is an informal, pre-mathematical notion
explanation: It links formal and informal concepts — evidence, not proof, supports it.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: Lambda calculus, general recursive functions and Turing machines were shown to be:
explanation: Independent formalisms converging — the thesis's strongest evidence.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: A universal Turing machine U takes as input:
options: An encoding ⟨M, w⟩ and simulates machine M running on w
explanation: One machine to run them all — the theoretical stored-program computer.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The UTM concept prefigured which practical idea?
options: The stored-program (von Neumann) computer — programs as data
explanation: Software = encoded machines executed by a fixed interpreter.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The language accepted by the universal TM, A_TM = {⟨M,w⟩ : M accepts w}, is:
explanation: Simulation semi-decides it; diagonalization kills decidability.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The diagonalization language L_d = {wᵢ : TM Mᵢ does NOT accept wᵢ} is:
explanation: If some Mⱼ recognized it, wⱼ yields a contradiction — the classic diagonal argument.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: Diagonalization as a proof technique was pioneered by:
options: Cantor (for uncountability), adapted by Turing and Gödel
explanation: The self-reference trick powering undecidability and incompleteness.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The number of Turing machines is countable while the number of languages is uncountable, hence:
options: Some (indeed most) languages have NO recognizing TM
explanation: A counting argument — non-RE languages must exist.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

topic: Reduction between languages and Rice's theorem
stem: A reduction A ≤m B lets us conclude:
options: B decidable ⇒ A decidable (and A undecidable ⇒ B undecidable)
explanation: Hardness flows forward, easiness flows backward through reductions.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

topic: Reduction between languages and Rice's theorem
stem: Rice's theorem states that every NONTRIVIAL property of the LANGUAGE recognized by a TM is:
explanation: Any semantic property that some TMs have and others lack cannot be decided.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

topic: Reduction between languages and Rice's theorem
stem: Which question is NOT covered by Rice's theorem (and is in fact decidable)?
options: Does M accept the empty string?
Does M have more than 100 states?
explanation: State count is a SYNTACTIC property of the machine, not of its language.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

topic: Reduction between languages and Rice's theorem
stem: To show E_TM (emptiness) undecidable, one typically reduces from:
explanation: Build M' accepting anything iff M accepts w — the standard construction.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The halting problem was proved undecidable by:
explanation: In the same paper that defined the machines.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: Which problem about CFGs is UNDECIDABLE?
options: Whether two CFGs generate the same language
explanation: Equivalence and ambiguity are undecidable; membership/emptiness are decidable.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The Post Correspondence Problem (PCP) is significant because:
options: It is a combinatorial undecidable problem used to prove undecidability of grammar problems
explanation: Domino matching reduces to CFG ambiguity/intersection questions.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: 'Does TM M halt on EVERY input?' (totality) is:
explanation: Universal quantification over inputs raises the difficulty a level.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: Practical consequences of undecidability include:
options: No general tool can perfectly detect infinite loops or verify arbitrary program properties
explanation: Static analysis must approximate — soundness vs completeness trade-offs.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: Hypercomputation proposals (machines beyond TM power) are viewed as:
options: Speculative — no physically realizable counterexample to the thesis is accepted
explanation: The thesis stands unrefuted after ninety years.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

topic: Reduction between languages and Rice's theorem
stem: In a mapping reduction A ≤m B, the reduction function f must be:
options: Computable, with w ∈ A ⟺ f(w) ∈ B
explanation: Effectiveness of f is what transfers (un)decidability.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: Interpreters and virtual machines in modern software are practical embodiments of:
explanation: Programs executing encoded programs.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The complement of the diagonalization language L_d is:
explanation: L̄_d = {wᵢ : Mᵢ accepts wᵢ} is recognizable by simulation.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: True or False: There exists no algorithm that decides, for every program and input, whether the program eventually halts.
explanation: True — the halting problem's undecidability.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

topic: Reduction between languages and Rice's theorem
stem: True or False: If A reduces to B and A is undecidable, then B must be undecidable.
explanation: True — a decider for B would yield one for A via the reduction.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem:
Assertion (A): New programming languages do not extend what is computable.
Reason (R): All Turing-complete formalisms compute exactly the same class of functions.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Expressiveness differs; computability does not — R explains A.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem:
Assertion (A): A perfect antivirus that decides maliciousness of every program cannot exist.
Reason (R): 'Exhibits malicious behaviour' is a nontrivial semantic property, undecidable by Rice's theorem.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Semantic detection reduces to undecidable questions — R explains A.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: Which problems are UNDECIDABLE? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: DFA questions are comfortably decidable.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

topic: Reduction between languages and Rice's theorem
stem: Which are SYNTACTIC (hence decidable) properties of a TM description? (Select all that apply.)
options: Whether it accepts a non-empty language
Whether it contains a transition on symbol 0
explanation: The fourth is semantic — Rice territory.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: Encoding a TM as a string ⟨M⟩ requires:
options: A systematic scheme listing states, alphabet and transitions in a finite description
explanation: Gödel-style encoding makes machines into data.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: 'REGULAR_TM = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) is regular}' is undecidable by:
options: Rice's theorem — regularity of L(M) is a nontrivial semantic property
explanation: A direct Rice application.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: Quantum computers, with respect to the Church-Turing thesis:
options: Compute the same class of functions, potentially faster for some problems
explanation: They challenge the EXTENDED (complexity) thesis, not computability itself.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

topic: Reduction between languages and Rice's theorem
stem: The property 'L(M) contains the string 101' is undecidable because:
options: It is a nontrivial property of the recognized language (some TMs have it, some don't)
explanation: Rice's theorem again — semantic and nontrivial.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: In the standard enumeration of TMs and strings used for L_d, every TM appears:
options: At some finite index in the enumeration
explanation: Effective enumeration of all machine encodings underpins diagonalization.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: 'Program verification is undecidable in general' means practical verifiers must:
options: Use approximations, restricted languages, or accept non-termination/incompleteness
explanation: Sound-but-incomplete tools, annotations and bounded checks are the engineering response.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The 'effective procedure' notion requires steps that are:
options: Finite, mechanical and definite, executable without insight
explanation: The informal notion the thesis formalizes.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: Minimal universal TMs (e.g. 2-state 3-symbol) demonstrate that:
options: Astonishingly small machines can be computationally universal
explanation: Wolfram's 2,3 machine proved universal in 2007.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: L̄_d (complement of the diagonal language) is RE but its complement is not, making the pair:
options: A witness that RE is not closed under complement
explanation: Asymmetry of semi-decidability in its purest form.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The CFG intersection-emptiness problem (is L(G1) ∩ L(G2) = ∅?) is:
explanation: A classic PCP consequence.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

topic: Reduction between languages and Rice's theorem
stem: Rice's theorem applies to properties of:
options: The language recognized by the machine
explanation: Semantic (language-level) properties only.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

stem: The 'extended' Church-Turing thesis concerns:
options: Efficiency — whether all reasonable models are polynomially equivalent to TMs
explanation: Quantum algorithms (Shor) are the main challenge to the extended version.
source: BEU syllabus — Formal Language & Automata Theory, Undecidability (7 hrs)

topic: What is Software Engineering and its history
stem: Software engineering is defined as:
options: The systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to developing, operating and maintaining software
explanation: IEEE's definition — engineering discipline applied to software.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

topic: What is Software Engineering and its history
stem: The term 'software engineering' was popularized at the:
options: 1968 NATO conference addressing the software crisis
explanation: Garmisch conference named the discipline.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The 'software crisis' referred to:
options: Projects exceeding budgets/schedules with poor quality and unmaintainable code
explanation: The 1960s realization that ad-hoc coding does not scale.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

stem: A root cause of the software crisis was:
options: Growing problem complexity outpacing informal development methods
explanation: Complexity demanded engineering discipline.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Evolution of a Programming System Product
stem: Brooks distinguishes a PROGRAM from a PROGRAMMING SYSTEMS PRODUCT, the latter costing roughly:
options: Nine times more (3× for productization × 3× for system integration)
explanation: The Mythical Man-Month's 3×3 estimate.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Unlike hardware, software:
options: Does not wear out but DETERIORATES through change; it is developed, not manufactured
explanation: The classic bathtub-curve contrast.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Software failure curves show increased failure rates after:
explanation: The 'spike' curve of modified software.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Brooks' No Silver Bullet, and Software Myths
stem: 'No Silver Bullet' argues that no single technology will give order-of-magnitude gains because:
options: ESSENTIAL complexity (the problem's inherent difficulty) dominates ACCIDENTAL complexity
explanation: Essence versus accident — Brooks 1986.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Brooks' No Silver Bullet, and Software Myths
stem: The software myth 'adding programmers to a late project helps' is refuted by:
options: Brooks's law — it makes the project later due to ramp-up and communication costs
explanation: Communication paths grow as n(n−1)/2.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Brooks' No Silver Bullet, and Software Myths
stem: The customer myth 'requirements can be vague; details come later' leads to:
options: Rework and cost explosion since defects found late cost far more to fix
explanation: Boehm's cost-of-change curve.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Software Development Life Cycles: Software Development Process
stem: A software process model defines:
options: The phases, activities and their ordering for developing software
explanation: The roadmap from concept to retirement.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

topic: The Code-and-Fix model, The Waterfall model, The Evolutionary Model
stem: The waterfall model arranges phases:
options: Sequentially — requirements → design → implementation → testing → maintenance
explanation: Royce's linear model with document-driven gates.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

topic: The Code-and-Fix model, The Waterfall model, The Evolutionary Model
stem: Waterfall's principal weakness is:
options: Late discovery of problems since working software appears only at the end and change is costly
explanation: Frozen requirements rarely match reality.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

topic: The Code-and-Fix model, The Waterfall model, The Evolutionary Model
stem: The code-and-fix model is characterized by:
options: Coding immediately without design, then patching problems as they surface
explanation: Fine for throwaway scripts, disastrous at scale.
source: BEU syllabus — Software Engineering, Unit 1

topic: The Code-and-Fix model, The Waterfall model, The Evolutionary Model
stem: The evolutionary model differs from waterfall by:
